overview: EC2 placement groups give you control over how instances are physically placed on AWS hardware, letting you trade latency against failure isolation. The section covers four strategies — cluster, spread, partition and precision time — each with a distinct limit and risk profile. For the exam, questions usually describe a workload requirement (low latency, high availability, rack-level isolation, accurate time) and expect you to pick the strategy and know its constraint numbers.

coreConcepts.definition: A logical grouping of EC2 instances that defines the placement strategy applied when the instances are launched.
Packs instances close together into a low-latency group within a single Availability Zone.
Places instances on distinct underlying physical hardware, reducing the risk of simultaneous failure, and can span Availability Zones.
Spreads instances across partitions that rely on different sets of racks within an AZ; a group can span multiple AZs in the same Region.
An isolated rack-set segment of a partition placement group; instances in one partition do not share racks with instances in other partitions.
Places instances on hardware with direct access to high-precision time sources such as enhanced Amazon Time Sync and a PTP hardware clock.
Networking option recommended for cluster placement groups; enables up to 10 Gbps bandwidth between instances.
AWS time source; in precision time groups the enhanced version is more accurate than standard NTP.
Precision Time Protocol hardware clock with hardware packet timestamping, available on Linux only, in precision time groups.
Partition information that instances in a partition placement group can access as instance metadata.

mustRemember: Cluster: instances are in a single Availability Zone; if the AZ fails, all instances in the group fail at the same time.
Cluster: up to 10 Gbps bandwidth between instances with Enhanced Networking enabled (recommended).
Spread: maximum 7 instances per group per Availability Zone.
Spread: instances sit on different physical hardware and the group can span Availability Zones.
Partition: up to 7 partitions per AZ, and a group can span multiple AZs in the same Region.
Partition: scales to hundreds of EC2 instances per group.
Partition: a partition failure can affect many EC2 instances but will not affect other partitions.
Partition instances can read their partition information as instance metadata.
Precision time: PTP hardware clock and hardware packet timestamping are Linux only.
When you create a placement group you must specify exactly one strategy.

keyComparisons.difference: Cluster maximizes network performance inside one AZ but all instances fail if the AZ fails; Spread minimizes simultaneous failure by using distinct hardware, capped at 7 instances per AZ.
Spread isolates every individual instance (limit 7 per AZ), while Partition isolates groups of instances by rack and scales to hundreds of instances.
Both are low-latency-friendly AZ-level placements, but Partition sacrifices close packing for rack isolation, while Cluster sacrifices failure isolation for 10 Gbps low latency.
Cluster addresses latency and bandwidth; precision time addresses clock accuracy (enhanced Time Sync, PTP) not throughput.

keyComparisons.items: Enhanced Time Sync vs standard NTP
keyComparisons.difference: The precision time group's enhanced Amazon Time Sync Service is more accurate than standard NTP, and it is paired with a Linux-only PTP hardware clock.

commonMisunderstandings: Spread groups are not unlimited across AZs — the cap is 7 instances per AZ per group, but the group itself can span AZs.
Partition is not the same as Spread: isolation is at rack/partition level, so a partition failure impacts all the instances in that partition.
Cluster placement groups are not highly available — they deliberately concentrate instances in one AZ.
Precision time is not about low network latency; it is about accurate time sources and timestamping.
A partition placement group is not limited to a single AZ — it can span multiple AZs within the same Region.
mentalModels: Cluster = one tightly packed rack room in one building: fast, but one fire takes everything.
Spread = each instance in its own separate building: maximum isolation, but only 7 per AZ.
Partition = several separate rack rooms: losing one room hurts that room only, not the others.
Precision time = a placement choice about clock accuracy, like giving instances a certified atomic watch.
Think of the placement strategy as deciding whether you are optimizing for speed, per-instance isolation, or failure-domain grouping.
edgeCases: Cluster's 10 Gbps figure applies between instances with Enhanced Networking enabled; Enhanced Networking is recommended, not automatic.
Partition group spanning is limited to multiple AZs in the same Region.
Partition metadata is available to instances inside the placement group as instance metadata, enabling distributed applications to be rack-aware.
PTP hardware clock support exists only on Linux instances.
Each placement group gets exactly one strategy at creation — you cannot mix strategies inside a group.

whenToUse.situation: Big Data job that must complete fast, or an application needing extremely low latency and high network throughput
Maximum high availability where each instance must be isolated from failures of the others
HDFS, HBase, Cassandra or Kafka needing rack-level isolation across hundreds of instances
Distributed database or financial workload needing accurate timestamps and event ordering
Workload must survive a single AZ failure
whenToUse.use: Spread or partition group (both can span AZs), not cluster

patternsToRecognize.signal: "10 Gbps between instances", "extremely low latency", "single AZ"
"each instance isolated from failure of the others", "maximize high availability", "limited number of critical instances"
"rack-aware", "HDFS/Cassandra/Kafka", "hundreds of instances", "partition failure affects only that partition"
"if the AZ fails all instances fail"

examTraps.trap: Cluster placement groups are the answer when the question demands both low latency and AZ-failure resilience.
examTraps.correction: Cluster is single-AZ; AZ failure fails every instance. Low-latency plus HA is not achievable with one cluster group.

examTraps.trap: Spread groups can hold unlimited instances because they span AZs.
examTraps.correction: The limit is 7 instances per AZ per placement group; spanning AZs does not remove the per-AZ cap.

examTraps.trap: Partition groups are limited to a single AZ like cluster groups.
examTraps.correction: Partition groups can span multiple AZs in the same Region, with up to 7 partitions per AZ and hundreds of instances.

examTraps.trap: Precision time groups are the choice for high-throughput networking.
examTraps.correction: Precision time is about clock accuracy; low latency and throughput are cluster territory.

examTraps.trap: Partition isolation means a failure hits only one instance.
examTraps.correction: A partition failure can affect many EC2 instances — but it will not affect other partitions.

beyondSource: Placement groups do not by themselves guarantee instance-type or capacity availability; capacity reservations or launch templates are separate considerations.
Cluster groups are commonly paired with other low-latency features (for example, EFA networking on supported instance types), but the source only cites Enhanced Networking and 10 Gbps.
